sentences.text: Tropeognathus possessed distinctively convex, keeled crests on the tip of its upper snout and a smaller mass on the underside of its lower jaws.

The upper crest extended from the snout tip back to the large opening on the side of the skull, giving the animal a broader skull than its relatives because the upper jaw crest was more prominent and much larger.
Its spine featured specialized fusions for stability: the first five dorsal vertebrae were joined into a structure called a notarium, while five sacral vertebrae were fused into a synsacrum.

The genus name Tropeognathus is derived from the Greek words for keel and jaw, while the species name mesembrinus is derived from the Greek for 'from the south', referring to its origin in the Southern Hemisphere.
Tropeognathus is considered the largest pterosaur found in the Southern Hemisphere, with an estimated wingspan of about 8.5 meters.

Later scientific analysis revised the maximum estimated wingspan of the large specimen used in media to 8.70 meters, identifying it as the largest known individual pterosaur based on its completeness.
The species Tropeognathus mesembrinus could have reached a wingspan of around 8.2 meters.
The genus Tropeognathus was described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1987, who named the type species Tropeognathus mesembrinus.
Fossils were found in the Romualdo Formation within the Santana Group in northeastern Brazil, specifically in the Romualdo Member of the Santana Formation.
In 2013, Alexander Kellner referred specimen MN 6594-1, a nearly complete skeleton, to Tropeognathus, a conclusion later supported by Taissa Rodrigues and Kellner.
Wellnhofer also named a second species, Tropeognathus robustus, in 1987.
The presence of convex, keeled crests on the snout and a mass on the lower jaw suggests these features played a role in the animal's display or social interactions.

Tropeognathus is classified within the family Anhangueridae, though some studies place it in Ornithocheiridae, creating a debate regarding family classification with some European researchers preferring the latter.
Recent analyses in 2019 and 2020 place Tropeognathus in the subfamily Tropeognathinae within Anhangueridae, as a sister taxon to Siroccopteryx.
The genus belongs to the family Ornithocheiridae, also known as Anhangueridae, and was a close relative of the species in the genus Anhanguera.
Fossils of Tropeognathus date to the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage, when the animal lived in South America during the late Early Cretaceous.
Tropeognathus lived during the Cretaceous period in South America.

Researchers have debated the validity of Tropeognathus, often reassigning its fossils to other genera like Anhanguera or Ornithocheirus, but in 2013 researchers concluded that Tropeognathus is a valid genus containing only the species T. mesembrinus.
